 These are the reasons for the determ ination regarding the claim to be a “Convention refugee”
1 presented by XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX a 23 year-old citizen of Malaysia, who has a lleged a well-founded fear of persecution by reasons of his religion, race and membership in a particular social group. THE ALLEGATIONS The following is a summary of the alle ged facts taken from the claimant’s Personal Information Form (PIF)
2 and his oral testimony, which is relevant for consideration in the claim: The claimant is a Tamil Hindu of Indian origin who came from XXXXXXXXXXX, Penang. He has 15 year s of schooling; and had been employed as technician in two establishments in Malaysia. The claimant testified that in Malaysia there exists discrimination against Tamil-Hindu Indians, especially in the areas of employment and education. He alleged that he was one of the seven Tamil-Hindu students who successfully completed a certificate program at the co llege level in 1996. Towards the end of his college program, all the seven Indians students were offered a government scholarship to continue their studies if they agree to convert to Islam. The claimant consented to conversion, and was granted a scholarship to study in a 3- year diploma program in XXXXXXXX XXX at the University XXXXXXXXXX Malaysia which began in XXXX 1997. In XXXXXXXX 1997, the claimant was approached by the Malaysian Islamic Youth Organization (ABIM), demandi ng him to convert to Islam as it was the condition for his scholarship. The clai mant responded that he had changed his mind about conversion. Since this incident, he was subjected to harassment in the campus. In XXXXXXX 1998, the claimant wa s notified that his scholarship was terminated because of his failure to fulfil requirement
3. The claimant could no longer afford to pay the cost of his study in the university without the scholarship, and so in XXX 1998 he quitted the program. From XXXX 1998 to XXXXXXXX 1999, the claimant obtained a part-time job in Butterworth and studied in another educational institution. On October 30, 1999, the claimant XX leged that a group of 3 Muslim- Malays stopped him outside of school cam pus and threatened him to convert or else be killed. On November 19, 1999, he was again approached by 6 Malays who insisted that he go to the mosque with them. When the claimant refused, he was beaten. The claimant and his father went to complain at the police station, but

- 2 - M99-11668 
 received no help. Upon his return home, his mother told him that someone had posed death threats against him on the phone. Fearful for his safety, the claimant left Malaysia for Canada where his father’s friend resided. He arrived in Toronto on November 26, 1999, and claimed refugee status in Montreal on November 28, 1999. ANALYSIS After having assessed the evidence as a whole, the panel finds plausibility and state protection to be the determinative issues in the claim. Although there were no significant c ontradictions or inconsistencies between the claimant’s PIF and his te stimony, the panel harbours serious doubt about the plausibility that he was pressured to convert to Islam on numerous occasions as the allegation is not supported by the following documentary evidence. Exhibit A-6 is a Response to Information Request on the subject of forced conversions to Islam of members of the minority religious communities since 1995, prepared by the Documentation, Info rmation Research Directorate (DIRB) of the Immigration and Refugee Board (I RB). After consulting twelve credible sources including Amnesty International and Human Rights World Report, this response quotes two Malaysia specialists and university professors, who stated that they are not aware of any cases of non-Muslims in Malaysia being forced to convert to Islam. Country Report on Human Rights Practices for 1999
4 states that the Constitution of Malaysia provides for freedom of religion; that religious minorities generally worship freely although with some restrictions. It further states that Islam is the official religion and that the government’s official policy is to “infuse Islamic values” into administration of matters, but does not impose Islamic law beyond the Muslim community. Exhibit P-21 is a document entitled “Prime Minister of Malaysia answers questions”, and is submitted by the claima nt for the purpose of establishing the “inception of Islamic values” in administra tion in his country. However, it is to be noted that the ending part of the document states: “[…] based on all the objective it is clear th at it is not to islamize the citizens of Malaysia who are not Muslims but to enhan ce the values of Islam to the values of the other religion is already teaching.[…]”
5 
(as per original, with omissions and errors)

 The above quotation again reinforced the fact that although the Malaysian government put in place Islamic values in its administration and policies, the intent is not to proselyte non-Muslims. In addition, another document stat es that Malaysia has “earned a reputation for its open, tolerant and ev en progressive system of Islamic practice”(IPS 25 Aug. 1997)
6. In 1998, the government announced that the “apostates”, that is, those who wish to leave or have left Islam for another religion, would not face government punishme nt as long as they did not defame Islam after their conversion.
7 Based on the above-mentioned document ary evidence, the panel is not persuaded that the claimant was forced to convert to Islam as he alleged. In the alternative, even if the claimant were credible, the issue of state protection would be a crucial element in determining whether his fear is well founded. Malaysia is a country with a parliamentary system of government based on periodic multi-party elections, and the st ate apparatus is functioning. In refugee determination, states are presumed capable of protecting their citizens, except in situations where the state is in a condition of complete breakdown. Absent an admission by the state that it is unable to protect, the claimant has the burden of presenting “clear and convincing evidence”
8 that state protection would not be reasonably forthcoming. The claimant testified that following his attack by the Muslim Malays in November 1999, he and his father went to report the incident to the police. He said that the sergeant asked him a lot of questions, but declined to file a report since the attackers could not be identified. The sergeant further told him that his situation was a case of racial tension, and that he would inform the leaders of the community, as he knew them. Although the panel finds that the sergeant could have documented the claimant’s complaint, however, his failure to do so is not “clear and convincing” evidence that he is denied of state protection available to him. The panel notes that the sergeant did seek information from the claimant about his problems, and that he offered to bring the issue to the attention of the leaders in the community. Furthermore, according to Human Rights World Report 1999,
9 the Malaysian government places a “high prio rity on preventing communal violence and punishing any activities seen as a possibl e incitement to violence. It is also said to be “wary of …extremist brands of Islam”, and quick to warn religious leaders against overzealous interpreta tion of Islamic law (IPS 25 Aug. 1997). 
2000 CanLII 21374 (CA IRB)
- 4 - M99-11668 
 Following the March 1998 clash between Muslims and Hindus in front of a mosque near George town, the capital of Penang State, police had reportedly arrested 107 people and seized various weapons.
10 The panel came to the conclusion that the claimant did not discharge his burden of proof by “clear and convincing ev idence” to rebut the presumption that state protection is available to him. Counsel submitted that as member of the religious minorities, the claimant encountered various forms of discrimi nation over the years, and that by cumulative effect, this would amount to persecution. The panel recognizes that the government implements extensive preferential programs to boost the economic position of the Malay majority, and that such programs and policies limit opportunities for non-Malays in hi gher education, government employment, business permits and license, and ownership of land
11. Nevertheless, the claimant has attained 15 years of education; he had no difficulties in his employment operated by Muslim-Malays. His scholarsh ip was terminated based on the fact that he did not convert to Muslim, a cr iteria which he was fully aware of and accepted. The panel finds insufficient eviden ce to demonstrate that he suffered discrimination which amounts to persecution. DETERMINATION For all these reasons, the pane l determines that by XXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXX is not a “Convention refugee” as defined in section 2 (1) of the Immigration Act. QueeXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX
